title: SECTION V — LANGUAGE
summary: Language becomes both subject and instrument of inquiry. The poems ask how thought finds its own speech, how inherited words carry new questions, and how individual, society, culture, knowledge and art meet inside language. The later, longer pieces widen this inquiry into humanity, value, visible and invisible realities, and the ethical possibilities of understanding.

entries.title: The Language That Makes Its Home Within
entries.summary: A meditation on language & meaning, knowledge & reason and earth & natural imagery. It moves from language & meaning toward knowledge & reason, allowing the poem’s emphasis to change as it develops. Close reading (PDF p. 322; printed p. 321): Language shelters generational memory, but the poem’s home must accommodate present intellectual work. Science, law and difficult philosophical questions belong there alongside inherited affection. A language kept only for display would lose this range of action. The poem joins emotional belonging to practical capacity: its future depends on what speakers can ask, explain and create in it. Respect for one language does not require diminishing another.

entries.title: Maithili's New Field
entries.summary: A meditation on language & meaning, knowledge & reason and work & material life. The recurring register of earth and plant imagery helps carry the poem’s movement. Close reading (PDF p. 323; printed p. 322): The new field is a field of use. Coining, borrowing and reviving words are practical responses to the need to speak about unfamiliar things. Translation must also give a work room to live in its receiving language. The poem’s advocacy of Maithili is therefore more demanding than ceremonial pride: readers and institutions must actually use it across domains. Expansion of that capacity can proceed alongside respect for other languages.

entries.title: When Thought Finds Its Own Speech
entries.summary: A meditation on knowledge & reason, language & meaning and time & impermanence. The recurring register of roads and journeys helps carry the poem’s movement. Close reading (PDF p. 324; printed p. 323): Inherited philosophical questions enter a wider public when thought finds language in which people can work with them. The poem connects this task to modern intellectual life and asks more of learning than success in examinations. Translation matters, but it is not the endpoint: new questions must also be produced. Its concern is the passage from receiving an intellectual inheritance to participating in its further development.

entries.title: New Questions in Old Letters
entries.summary: A meditation on knowledge & reason, language & meaning and body & consciousness. It moves from knowledge & reason toward language & meaning, allowing the poem’s emphasis to change as it develops. Close reading (PDF p. 325; printed p. 324): Older letters need not imprison the questions asked through them. The poem presents inherited philosophical language as a medium of continuing debate, with precision available for new problems. Questioning a tradition is consequently different from dismissing it. The reader is invited to test whether an old distinction still clarifies a present difficulty. Respect becomes intellectually productive when it includes the labour of definition, disagreement and renewed application.

entries.title: From Roots to Horizon
entries.summary: A meditation on knowledge & reason, time & impermanence and earth & natural imagery. It moves from knowledge & reason toward time & impermanence, allowing the poem’s emphasis to change as it develops. Close reading (PDF p. 326; printed p. 325): Roots locate thought, while the horizon draws it toward questions beyond an inherited boundary. The poem approaches comparison through the illumination offered by different traditions rather than through a contest to declare one superior. Contemporary problems give this encounter practical urgency. Its figure of the scholar as a connecting presence suggests a double responsibility: understand the materials received closely, and make them available for inquiry into a changing world.
